newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Liberals reverse slide - Reuters poll.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Liberals reverse slide - Reuters poll.

text.p: Canada's ruling Liberal Party, fighting to retain its majority in the June 2 election, has regained some momentum after a steady slide in voter support earlier this week, a Reuters poll showed on Thursday.

The last of five daily tracking polls conducted for Reuters by Zogby International showed support for Prime Minister Jean Chretien's Liberals rising to 41.9 percent from 39.7 percent in Wednesday's poll.
"It appears the Liberal support has stopped its downward slide," pollster John Zogby said in a telephone interview.
"It appears that the Liberals are headed toward a majority (and) that Reform, on the basis of its strength in the West, should win the second greatest number of seats," he said.
Reuters-Zogby polls earlier in the week threw into question the Liberals' ability to win another outright majority.
In the 1993 election, the Liberals won 177 of the 295 seats in the House of Commons on 41 percent of the vote.

Thursday's poll showed support for the right-wing Reform Party slipping to 17.3 percent from 17.5 percent the previous day. Conservative Party support also weakened slightly to 21.3 percent from 21.5 percent previously.
Nevertheless, Reform appears poised to displace the separatist Bloc Quebecois as the official opposition in Canada's Parliament, according to the poll.
Reform's strength is centered in the Western provinces of Alberta and British Columbia, while Conservative backing is scattered in pockets across Quebec, Ontario and the Atlantic provinces.

In French-speaking Quebec, the latest Reuters poll showed Bloc Quebecois support jumping to 36 percent from 29 percent in Wednesday's poll. It is still a three-way race in the province, however, with the Liberals at 32 percent and the Conservatives at 30 percent.
"It's very close in Quebec," Zogby said. "It's a dog fight."
The Reuters poll on Thursday showed the Liberals with a huge lead in vote-rich Ontario and in the Prairies and the Maritimes.
Reform led the Liberals in Alberta by 47 percent to 26 percent and in British Columbia by 36 percent to 34 percent.
The undecided vote was still substantial, Zogby said. Thursday's poll showed 23.7 percent undecided, compared with a high of 32.6 percent on Monday.
"Traditionally, undecided voters break against the incumbent and do so over the last couple of days,"" Zogby said.

The new poll of 1,056 Canadians was taken from Monday through Wednesday. It has a margin of error of 3.1 percentage points at a confidence level of 95 percent. The margin of error is higher for regional breakdowns.
Canadian election law prohibits the publication of polls 72 hours before voting day.
